name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

territory.border: hb:1914:United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

areaKm2.note: Published area of Great Britain and Ireland ~315,000 km2 (B&H Table 1: 0.3M km2); the world_1914 polygon computes to ~323,000 km2 (high).

population.note: Broadberry and Harrison 2005 Table 1: United Kingdom (incl. all Ireland) 1913 = 46.0M; COW tpop 1914 = 46,048k; OWID/HYDE 1914 45.6M (low, present-day borders). Empire excluded (British colonies 380M, Dominions 19.9M).

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share UK 1910 = 65.6% (incl. Ireland); England and Wales 1911 census 78% urban districts. Mid 0.75 for the UK incl. less urban Ireland. Low/high span the definitions.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. Army figures read from the cited British Army page; navy figures recalled from Halpern, not read from a fetched source. Cited page: 247,432 regulars in August 1914, Army Reserve 145,347, Special Reserve 64,000 and Territorial Force ~246,000, 'a mobilised force of almost 700,000'; plus 300,000 volunteers enlisted in August (untrained, not counted). Royal Navy ~146,000 active plus ~100,000 mobilised reservists (Halpern ch. 1). Snapshot month: August 1914. Check: COW NMC v7 milper 1914 = 532k, 1915 = 4,350k (annual averages, not the snapshot-date strength).

trainedReserves.note: Cited page: National Reserve 215,000 men with prior service, of whom ~60,000 classed as willing and able to serve. Kitchener volunteers (750,000 by end of September) were untrained and belong to the mobilizable pool.

supportPersonnel.note: Royal Navy and Royal Marines (~250,000 mobilised), artillery, engineers, Army Service Corps, RFC, depots and staffs; the infantry share of the BEF was 64.6% (cited page).

mobilizationRatio.note: Over the war ~5.7M served in the army and ~0.6M in the navy and air force from the UK (incl. Ireland: 206,000 Irishmen, World War I casualties page); 5,399,563 men served with the BEF (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Expeditionary_Force_(World_War_I)). ~6.1M / 46M = 0.13.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: 157 regular battalions (~1,000 each, 74 of them overseas) and ~200 Territorial battalions (~800) per the cited page; ~157,000 + ~160,000.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: SMLE rifle; 2 MGs per battalion; no heavy howitzers at division level

training.note: Rubric row: training 1.0 (elite long-service professionals). Evidence: regulars trained to 15 aimed rounds per minute (Mons, Le Cateau); Territorials part-time

count.note: 31 regular cavalry regiments (12 overseas) on the cited page, ~550 sabres each, plus ~55 Yeomanry regiments. Armed with the infantry rifle and able to fight dismounted.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: full rifle, not carbine (cited page)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: dismounted fire training after the Boer War

count.note: Division establishment on the cited page: 54 18-pdr, 18 4.5-in howitzers and 4 60-pdr per division (76 guns); 6 regular BEF divisions + 1 cavalry = ~480 guns, home and overseas regular batteries, and 14 Territorial divisions with 15-pdr and 5-in howitzers. Reconstruction, grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: 18-pdr QF good; very few heavy guns; shrapnel-heavy ammunition

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: regular Royal Artillery

count.note: Cited page: the RFC had 179 aeroplanes at the outbreak (84 with the Military Wing per the British Army page); the RNAS had ~90 aircraft and 7 airships. The BEF took ~30 serviceable machines to France (Aviation in WWI page). Unarmed reconnaissance types; no fighters existed.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: B.E.2, Avro 504, Bleriot; dependent on French engines

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: RFC reconnaissance found von Kluck's turn at Mons

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Halpern, A Naval History of World War I (isbn:1-55750-352-4), not read from a fetched source. Battleships, cruisers and destroyers. Halpern ch. 1 and Conway's 1906-1921: ~22 dreadnoughts (incl. Agincourt and Erin seized in August), 9 battlecruisers, ~40 pre-dreadnoughts, ~34 armoured cruisers and ~80 protected, scout and light cruisers = 160/180/190, low drops ships in reserve; plus ~221 destroyers in commission in August 1914 (Halpern ch. 1) = 200/220/230. Role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: destroyers moved from ships_minor, which is now omitted (torpedo boats and sloops stay excluded).

quality.note: Count-weighted mean (mid counts) of battleships/cruisers 0.8/0.85/0.9 (180) and destroyers 0.75/0.8/0.85 (220), role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries. Rubric rows: quality 0.75-1.0 (the era's best) and 0.75. Evidence: largest dreadnought fleet with 13.5-in and 15-in guns, large modern destroyer flotillas; shell and magazine flaws shown at Jutland

training.note: Count-weighted mean (mid counts) of battleships/cruisers (180) and destroyers (220), both 0.75/0.8/0.85, role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries. Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: long-service professional navy; signalling weaknesses

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. ~74-77 submarines in commission (Conway's 1906-1921), mostly coastal B-, C- and D-class; 8 E-class overseas boats.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: E class good; most boats coastal

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: E-boats operated in the Baltic and Marmara in 1915

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: competent but inexperienced at corps level; Sir John French's wavering at the Marne; Admiralty strong

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75-1.0. Evidence: regimental system; old regulars fought on at Mons, Le Cateau and First Ypres until destroyed

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75 (motivated). Evidence: volunteer rush, 300,000 enlistments in August (cited page)

weapons.note: Anchor: 7 (1905). Evidence: SMLE, Vickers MG, 18-pdr QF; little heavy artillery

armor.note: Anchor: 7 (armoured cars, steel helmet 1915). Evidence: RNAS armoured cars from autumn 1914; Brodie helmet 1915

ships.note: Anchor: 7 (dreadnoughts). Evidence: Queen Elizabeth class (15-in, oil-fired) completing; director firing; the world's largest navy audit 2026-10-30: mid 7.4 -> 7.24, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 1914 (7.237); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

fortification.note: Anchor: 7 (concrete forts). Evidence: coastal forts at Portsmouth, Plymouth, Rosyth; little land fortification

logistics.note: Anchor: 7 (railways). Evidence: dense rail network, motor transport in the ASC, world's largest merchant fleet

communications.note: Anchor: 7 (telegraph, telephone). Evidence: global cable network, naval wireless, Room 40 codebreaking from late 1914

isr.note: Anchor: ISR 7 = aerial reconnaissance. Evidence: RFC reconnaissance, naval intelligence

air.note: Anchor: air 7 = 1914. Evidence: B.E.2, early seaplanes and RNAS raids on Zeppelin sheds (Aviation in WWI page)

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID CSV): UK 1913 = 8,212, 1914 = 8,131 (2011 int$). B&H Table 1: 4,921 in 1990 int$.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Mid read from Broadberry and Harrison Table 5; low recalled from Ferguson, not read from a fetched source. Low ~3.1% of NNP in 1913 (Ferguson table 6). Mid: B&H Table 5 government spending 23.5% of GDP in 1914 (8.2% in 1913), less civil spending. High: 52.4% in 1915.

industrialShare.note: Industry and mining ~40-45% of GDP; agriculture only ~7% of output (Broadberry and Howlett in Broadberry and Harrison 2005, ch. 7). Grade C.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - a / s (a = agricultural share of employment, s = calorie self-sufficiency). a: Herrendorf et al. via OWID, United Kingdom agriculture share of employment 1911 = 11.8%, 1920 = 8.6%. s: "Before the War about 60 percent of the energy value of the British diet was derived from foodstuffs that were imported" (Gazeley and Newell 2010, IZA DP 5297, p. 11, https://repec.iza.org/dp5297.pdf); 58% of calories in 1913 (Offer, as summarised in https://www.habselstree.org.uk/boys/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2024/06/OP65StJohnFoodSupplyandWorldWarOne.pdf); 64% (https://shipwreckedmariners.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Why-Britain-Wasnt-Starved-into-Surrender-in-WW1.pdf). Mid 1 - 0.118/0.40 = 0.70. Low a 0.125, s 0.36 = 0.65; high a 0.11, s 0.42 = 0.74. Grade C: two sources combined. Import dependence: ~60% of calories imported, four fifths of wheat. audit 2026-10-30: was 0.87/0.88/0.9 (s = 1 assumed); fetched s applied.

annualCohort.note: ~1.15M births per year in the 1890s (UK incl. Ireland), half male, ~75% survival to 20. Volunteer army until conscription in 1916.

aircraft_fighter.note: Cited page: 52,000 aeroplanes produced in total by 1918, i.e. ~12,000 per year over 1915-18 rising to ~30,000 in 1918 (the page's line '200 in 1914 to 3,200 in 1918' is inconsistent with that total and not used). Fighter share an educated split.

aircraft_strike.note: Reconnaissance and bomber share of the totals above.

artillery.note: Cited page: annual output of artillery grew from 91 guns in 1914 to 8,039 in 1918; 25,000 artillery pieces in total.

armor.note: Cited page: 2,800 tanks built by 1918 (from 1916); ~1,400 per year in 1917-18.

ships_major.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Battleships, battlecruisers, light cruisers and destroyers completed per year: capital ships and light cruisers 1914-1918 = 4/8/12 (Conway's); destroyers 1915-1918 = 50/70/100 (~300 over the war). Role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: destroyers moved from ships_minor, which is now omitted.

submarines.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Submarines completed per year 1915-1918.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Metalled roads of Great Britain and Ireland.

railKm.note: CHAT railline United Kingdom: 1913 = 32,623 km. The file does not state whether Ireland is included; the Irish network is not added.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Halpern, A Naval History of World War I (isbn:1-55750-352-4), not read from a fetched source. London, Liverpool, Glasgow, Southampton, Portsmouth, Plymouth, Rosyth, Scapa Flow, Harwich, Cardiff, Newcastle, Hull, Belfast, Dover, Queenstown.

merchantTonnage.note: Lloyd's Register returns 1914: United Kingdom 18,696,237 GRT (vessels of 100 tons and over, Register Book 1913-14); British colonies add 1,735,306 GRT (excluded). Converted to deadweight at x1.5 (low x1.3 of the low GRT, high x1.6 of the high GRT).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Recalled from van Creveld, Supplying War (isbn:0-521-21730-X), not read from a fetched source. van Creveld ch. 4-5: rail and sea-supplied expeditionary force; motor lorries in the ASC.

draftAnimals.note: ~2.4M horses in the UK; the army impressed ~165,000 in August 1914. Grade C.

chokepoints: North Sea exits (Scapa Flow to Norway)

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: island base, Royal Navy, fortified naval ports, population support.

notes: Snapshot date August 1914 after mobilisation (war declared 4 Aug). United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland only: Indian Army, Dominion forces and colonial populations excluded, includes empty. Forces include the ~74 regular battalions garrisoned overseas. The BEF in France in August was 6 infantry and 1 cavalry division (~120,000-150,000 men) with ~480 guns. Aircraft in aircraft_strike (no fighters in 1914). Ship convention per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: battleships, carriers, cruisers and destroyers = ships_major, torpedo boats and smaller craft = ships_minor (role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries). Book figures (Halpern, Conway's) not fetched online, graded at most B.
